title: On-call & Incident Response Central Playbook
author: Priya Raman
content:
Summary:
This playbook is Redwood Inference's canonical on-call and incident response reference. It consolidates incident severity definitions, triage and escalation procedures, core runbooks for frequent failure modes, postmortem and RCA guidance, on-call rotation rules, game day planning, and status page / customer communication templates. Intended audience: on-call engineers, SREs, incident commanders, and engineering managers.

Scope:
- Applies to all production-facing services (api-gateway, inference-runtime, routing-service, kv-cache, redwood-console) and external customer-facing incidents.
- Not an exhaustive technical runbook for every service; links to per-service runbooks are provided in Related pages.

1) Incident severity definitions (single source of truth)
- P0 (Sev-0): Complete outage or data loss affecting all customers or critical business flows. Examples: inference-runtime OOM across autoscale group, primary DB corrupted.
- P1 (Sev-1): Major degradation impacting a large percentage of traffic or a high-severity customer. Examples: sustained p95 latency > 2x SLO, error rate > 5% for > 5 minutes.
- P2 (Sev-2): Partial degradation or feature loss affecting a subset of customers or non-critical flows.
- P3 (Sev-3): Informational / minor issues, cosmetic bugs, or scheduled maintenance notes.

SLO & trigger thresholds (for automated alerting):
| Service | SLO (availability) | Alert threshold | Pager severity |
| api-gateway | 99.95% | 5m error rate > 1% | P1 |
| inference-runtime | 99.9% | p95 latency > 500ms for 3m | P1 |
| routing-service | 99.95% | request drops > 0.5% for 5m | P1 |
| kv-cache | 99.9% | cache miss spike > 10x baseline for 5m | P2 |

2) Detection, Triage & Initial Actions (first 15 minutes)
1. Acknowledge the pager (PagerDuty). If automatic acknowledgements are configured, confirm with `pd incidents show`.
2. Triage: determine scope (service, region, percent of traffic), and severity using definitions above.
3. Run quick checks (check dashboards, recent deploys, alerting runbook snippets):
   - Dashboards: api-gateway p95/p99, error-rate, request-rate, infra GPU node health, autoscaler status.
   - Deployments: `git log`/CI recent deploys, check recent Canary -> Full rollout state in Redwood Console.
   - Logs: use `kubectl logs` / `gcloud logging read` equivalent; filter by errors and stack traces.
4. If P0/P1, escalate to Incident Commander (IC) immediately and start an incident channel (Slack #incident-<short-id>).
5. Notify SRE lead and on-call engineering manager.

Escalation matrix (example):
- Pager fires -> primary on-call engineer (10 min ack) -> secondary on-call (10 min) -> SRE lead -> Eng manager -> CTO.
- For P0, IC must be identified within first 5 minutes and PG (postmortem guardian) assigned within first 30 minutes.

3) Incident roles & responsibilities
- Initial Responder: first engineer to acknowledge and run triage checklist.
- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates the incident, owns the timeline and external communications.
- Communications Lead: drafts internal and customer-facing updates.
- Technical Lead(s): implement mitigating actions and fixes.
- Postmortem Author: documents RCA and corrective actions after severity P1/P0.

4) Core runbooks (quick links & primary steps)
A. High API latency (api-gateway / inference-runtime)
- Symptoms: p95 > 2x SLO or customer reports of slowness.
- Quick checks:
  - Check autoscaler: `kubectl get hpa -n inference` and node utilization.
  - Inspect model-serving pods for OOMs / restarts: `kubectl describe pod <pod>`
  - Check KV cache hit rate and TTLs (cache stampedes may increase latency).
- Mitigations (in order):
  1. Roll back recent model or runtime deploy if rollout correlated with onset.
  2. Increase autoscaler min-replicas (temporary): update HPA or scale statefulset.
  3. Enable degraded-mode routing: shift traffic to lower-latency region or to a lighter quantized model variant.
  4. Clear large KV-cache hotspots if safe: `redis-cli CLIENT LIST` + selective `DEL` keys.
  5. If resource starvation (GPU mem), reduce batch size via feature-flagged runtime config.
- Post-incident: collect flamegraphs, pprof, and model KV cache stats.

B. GPU node down / instance failure
- Symptoms: node NotReady, multiple pods pending scheduling.
- Quick checks:
  - `kubectl get nodes` and cloud provider console for instance health.
  - Check cluster autoscaler & spot instance eviction logs.
- Mitigations:
  1. Drain and reprovision node: `kubectl cordon <node>` then `kubectl drain <node>`; investigate underlying instance failure in cloud console.
  2. Trigger manual scale-up of reserved pool or move critical pods to dedicated nodes.
  3. If using spot instances, failover to on-demand pool for critical traffic.

C. Model OOM or KV cache corruption
- Symptoms: inference-runtime pod OOMKilled during long contexts; cache miss storms; inconsistent responses.
- Quick checks and mitigations:
  - Restart model-serving pod(s) with lower max-sequence or reduced kv cache size.
  - Temporarily pin inference requests to smaller/quantized model.
  - If corruption suspected, invalidate and rebuild KV cache from source-of-truth.

D. Authentication / Authorization failures (customer API keys)
- Symptoms: large number of 401/403 responses; customer reports.
- Quick checks:
  - Check auth-service logs, key rotation jobs, KMS connectivity.
- Mitigations:
  1. Rollback recent auth or key-rotation changes.
  2. If KMS outage, switch to cached token fallback (documented fallback path).
  3. Notify Customer Success and prepare targeted customer comms.

5) Communications: internal & customer templates
- Internal Incident Channel message (first post):
  Subject: [INCIDENT] <short-id>











 - <service> - <P#> - <brief summary>
  Body: 1) Impact statement (who/what/where) 2) Initial triage (probable root cause or hypothesis) 3) Actions taken 4) Next steps / owner 5) IC & technical leads

- Public status page template (initial):
  Title: Degraded service for <service>
  Impact: We are experiencing elevated errors/latency impacting customers in <region>.
  What we know: Initial investigation points to <brief cause/hypothesis>
  Mitigation in progress: <high-level steps>
  Next update: <ETA or timebox, e.g., 30 mins>

- Customer-facing email / DM template (short):
  Subject: Service interruption affecting <product> (incident <short-id>)
  Body: Hi <Customer>, we’re aware of an issue affecting <impact>. Our on-call team is actively investigating. We will provide updates via status.redwood.ai/incidents/<short-id>. For urgent needs, reply to this message.

6) Postmortem & RCA process (P1/P0 mandatory)
- Timeline:
  - Incident declared resolved: IC closes incident and assigns Postmortem Author within 48 hours.
  - Draft postmortem due within 7 days. Final review and action items assigned within 14 days.
- Postmortem structure (required fields):
  - Title, incident ID, severity, timeline (minute-granular), impact (customers, revenue, SLO hits), root cause, contributing factors, corrective and preventive actions (owner + ETA), detection gap analysis, monitoring or alerting changes, and lessons learned.
- Postmortem review: mandatory 1-hour blameless review with stakeholders; action items tracked in JIRA and linked from postmortem.

7) On-call rotations & rules
- Rotation cadence: primary on-call rotates weekly; secondary rotates bi-weekly.
- Shift handover checklist (before shift end):
  - Confirm no open P1/P0 incidents assigned to you.
  - Update runbook notes with any outstanding mitigations.
  - Handoff message in #oncall-handoffs with current state and follow-ups.
- Rules:
  - Do not escalate directly to CTO unless P0 and chain-of-command is unavailable.
  - Document all mitigation steps in the incident channel for auditability.
  - Ensure contact info in PagerDuty is up to date (phone, Slack, backup).

8) Game days (regular preparedness exercises)
- Frequency: quarterly cross-functional game days (SRE, runtime, infra, customer success).
- Objectives: validate runbooks, test failover paths (region failover, model fallback), rehearse comms templates, and measure MTTR improvements.
- Post-game-day: capture findings, update runbooks, and assign action items.

9) Monitoring, observability & instrumentation requirements
- Every production service must emit: request latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate, request rate, CPU/GPU mem usage, and health checks.
- Key dashboards: Global SRE Overview, Inference Latency Heatmap, Autoscaler & GPU Utilization, Recent Deployments.
- Alerting policy: favor high-precision alerts for P0/P1, use aggregated low-noise alerts for P2/P3.

10) Post-incident follow-ups & metrics to track
- MTTR (mean time to recovery) per severity.
- Number of recurring incidents by root cause category (deploy, infra, model, config, external).
- Percent of incidents with RCA & action items closed within 30 days.
- Alert fatigue metrics: # of alerts per on-call per week; aim to reduce by 25% YoY.

Appendices:
A. Quick CLI snippets:
- Check recent deploys: `git log --since=24.hours --pretty=oneline`
- Kubernetes pod restarts: `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --sort-by=.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount`
- Draining node: `kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`

- Customer Success on-call: Laila Chen (cs-oncall@redwood.ai)

C. Templates & links

Change log:

If you are on-call and uncertain about the next step, escalate to the IC and SRE lead — faster coordination reduces customer impact.
